taunsa-barrage-basti-shaikhan-relocation.community: The project's feasibility study, detailed designs and environmental impact assessment all concluded that the works would cause no land acquisition and no involuntary resettlement. At mobilisation the ICB-01 contractor asked for a change of working areas, which required moving two villages living on embankment land owned by the Irrigation and Power Department on both banks of the Indus beside the barrage. The Department agreed without consulting the Bank, 'rushed through the relocation planning process and moved the two villages in June 2005 to two new sites within half a kilometer distance'. The completion report states that this 'did not follow World Bank Operation Policy (OP 4.12) on Involuntary Resettlement' and that the relocation 'was rushed without adequate consultation and planning'. The Bank learned of it from a local non-governmental organisation in July 2005, sent investigative missions, and required a resettlement action plan, which was approved in November 2005, five months after the move. The plan covered 160 households, 137 on the left bank and 23 on the right, about 900 people, living on Department land without title and working as fishermen on the contractors' boats, at odd jobs, and making brooms and baskets. All 160 households built their own houses with the compensation money and moved in; the two new sites cover about 2.8 hectares. The project then provided open sewage drains, community toilets with showers, flushing latrines, household electricity, a link road, paved streets, a mosque and schools, and a 12-bed basic health unit handed to the District Health Department. The Independent Evaluation Group records that 'As a result of pressure from NGOs and the Bank an emergency Resettlement Action Plan was formulated and implemented, albeit with some delays and need for improved procedures to redress grievances'. The Japan Center for a Sustainable Environment and Society, which investigated in the field, wrote to Bank staff on 26 October 2006 that 'all displaced families in Basti Sheikhan have received Rs 40,000' while 'families in Basti Allah Wali have received only Rs 16,000 regardless of house sizes and types', against a plan under which payments were to vary with the size and type of the house; that displaced people 'had been facing serious water stagnation in their houses and gardens'; that 'Construction of walls is not included in the compensation for displaced people'; that at Basti Sheikhan one toilet was being used by three families; and that '38 Villagers in Basti Allah Wali are facing court cases filed by the Government of Pakistan'. Dawn reported on 9 May 2006 that people affected by the project protested at the resettlement site during a World Bank delegation's visit, said compensation for displaced fishermen 'ranged only from Rs16,000 to Rs40,000', and 'claimed that many of those displaced had still not received the compensation'. The same works also closed the irrigation canals. The completion report states that the contractor's work plans did not aim at minimum canal closures, that the canals stayed closed for extended periods 'causing distress, particularly to a part of the D.G. Khan Canal command area during the rabi cropping season of 2005-06', and that the Project Management Office did not tell farmers in the D.G. Khan and Muzaffargarh canal commands in advance so that they could adjust their farming or find other water. A Punjab Rural Support Programme assistance package of subsidised wheat seed, hand pumps, community infrastructure, microcredit and skills training followed. Twenty years later, in January 2026, Dawn reported that 150 armed policemen with two bulldozers arrived at the same riverside settlement of the Mohana boat people, on 47 kanal of state land marked on an official map as 'proposed for Circuit House'. Asad Farooq of the Alternative Law Collective told the paper that 'the families were moved two thousand feet away in the first wave of evictions' and were not granted legal rights over the land they were moved to.
taunsa-barrage-basti-shaikhan-relocation.displaced_label: 160 households, 137 on the left bank and 23 on the right, about 900 people, physically relocated in June 2005 and resettled under the November 2005 resettlement action plan (World Bank completion report, 1 June 2010)
taunsa-barrage-basti-shaikhan-relocation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 799 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The nearest figure in a document is the Japan Center for a Sustainable Environment and Society's reading of the resettlement action plan of 29 November 2005, which it gives as 157 households and 799 people. The Bank's own completion report gives 160 families, 137 on the left bank and 23 on the right, 'comprising of some 900 people'. No document found explains the gap between 157 and 160 households or between 799 and about 900 people.
taunsa-barrage-basti-shaikhan-relocation.suppression: Dawn reported on 12 August 2006 that scores of riverine residents displaced by the project protested in Multan against 'the alleged highhandedness of an engineering firm', identified as Descon, which had kept working late at night after residents asked it to stop, disturbing people and particularly women who were sleeping outdoors after being displaced, and whose staff reportedly harassed residents of Allahwali Basti. The same report records that a case was filed against some 15 people for allegedly obstructing construction work and that two of the accused were arrested. The Japan Center for a Sustainable Environment and Society's letter of 26 October 2006 records that 38 villagers in Basti Allah Wali were facing court cases filed by the Government of Pakistan. In January 2026, long after the loan closed, Dawn reported that 150 armed policemen and two bulldozers were sent to demolish the settlement, which the Punjab Enforcement and Regulatory Authority says was served with a digital Emergency Prohibition Order; the activist Fazl-e-Rab said the settlement had no warning the bulldozers were coming, and an evicted resident, Muhammad Shareef, has a petition against the authority still being heard.
taunsa-barrage-basti-shaikhan-relocation.killed_note: No worker deaths are recorded in the completion report, the Independent Evaluation Group's review or the health and safety section of the report's environmental annex.
taunsa-barrage-basti-shaikhan-relocation.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2009 with the barrage rehabilitated and both villages rebuilt on Irrigation and Power Department land about half a kilometre from where they had stood. An independent consultant engaged by the Project Management Office evaluated the resettlement through a community survey, group meetings and interviews with key informants and concluded that it had mitigated the project's adverse impacts and improved the affected households' living conditions. The completion report's own lesson is that 'The initial simplistic and rushed approach skipped the required planning steps and led to many of the grievances and cost increases later.' Resettlement cost Rs 31.85 million against an initial estimate of Rs 12.42 million. The people moved were never given legal rights over the new land, and in January 2026 the Punjab Enforcement and Regulatory Authority sent police and bulldozers to clear the site.
taunsa-barrage-basti-shaikhan-relocation.ecosystem: The barrage sits inside the Taunsa Barrage Wildlife Sanctuary. A baseline survey of the sanctuary by WWF-Pakistan, submitted to the Project Management Office in August 2006, recorded about 25 Indus dolphins within 2.5 km of the barrage and 'noted that these appeared to have been displaced by the disturbance arising from project activities'. It also found that hog deer, endangered nationally, was at risk of becoming extinct within the sanctuary because the population was not viable and not connected to other populations, and listed resource extraction, hunting and fishing as threats. The completion report states that 'Not all recommendations of the report were implemented.' The death of two Indus dolphins near the barrage was reported in January 2006; WWF's final report concluded that only one dolphin was involved and that it was released into the river after becoming entangled in a fishing net, 'although its subsequent survival was uncertain'. Afterwards a community member was given a boat to patrol the area, contractor and consultant staff were trained in dolphin handling by the Sindh Wildlife Department, and the contractor set up a dolphin rescue team and employed a game watcher. An environmental audit in October 2008 found that overall environmental and social concerns were well addressed.

taunsa-barrage-basti-shaikhan-relocation.confidence_note: The relocation itself, its date, the breach of the Bank's resettlement policy and the 160 households all come from the Bank's own completion report, which is candid about them, and are repeated by the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The compensation amounts, the court cases against 38 villagers and the conditions at the new sites come from an independent source, the Japan Center for a Sustainable Environment and Society, which investigated in the field and wrote to Bank staff; the household count in its reading of the resettlement plan, 157, differs by three from the Bank's 160. The arrests, the harassment allegations and the Rs16,000 to Rs40,000 range are from two Dawn reports of May and August 2006. The compensation amounts in the Japanese-language factsheet of 28 November 2006 are garbled in the file and the English letter of 26 October 2006 is the better source for them. The 2026 police and bulldozer operation was carried out by the Punjab Enforcement and Regulatory Authority more than sixteen years after the loan closed and is not attributed here to the project; it is reported because it fell on the settlement the project created and because it turns on the lack of legal title the project left in place. No document found names any of the 160 households, states how long the canal closures lasted, or says how many farming households the closures affected.
taunsa-barrage-basti-shaikhan-relocation.drop_reason: Duplicate. The map already carries this project as taunsa-barrage-relocation (Taunsa Barrage, Indus River, Punjab, 2005-2009), which rests on the same loan, the same completion report and the same Independent Evaluation Group review, and already records the two villages moved in June 2005 at the contractor's request, the breach of OP 4.12, the 160 families and about 900 people, the canal closures, the JACSES report of 38 people indicted, and Descon's protest. The existing case carries no P-number, which is why dedupe_leads.py reported P088994 as new; the lead row's own _local_match flagged it at strength 3. Not written as a new case. See _extend_recommendation for the material that is genuinely new and was checked against the documents.

verified_new_material: The relocation cost: an initial RAP estimate of Rs 12.42 million (completion report, Annex 9, 'Initial RAP Cost'), Rs 14.704 million of the revised PC-1 provision of Rs 19.883 million actually spent on the RAP, plus Rs 17.150 million of community development works through the construction contractor, bringing the total to Rs 31.855 million (completion report, section 1, 'Involuntary resettlement').

The resettlement sites cover about 2.8 hectares and were laid out on Irrigation and Power Department land about 0.5 km from the old settlements; all households built their own houses with the compensation money; 137 households were resettled on the left bank and 23 on the right (completion report, Annex 9, 'RAP Implementation').
About 136 local people took work with the contractor, 66 of them project-affected persons (completion report, Annex 9).

JACSES letter to John Wall and Xiokai Li, 26 October 2006, verified in full on jacses.org: 'According to villagers of Basti Sheikhan ... and Basti Allah Wali, all displaced families in Basti Sheikhan have received Rs 40,000, and families in Basti Allah Wali have received only Rs 16,000 regardless of house sizes and types', against the plan's entitlement matrix; water stagnation in houses and gardens through the monsoon, with 25 families still without land-raising aggregates; walls not included in compensation, with women the direct victims of the lack of privacy; one toilet used by three families at Basti Sheikhan; houses built around a power pylon; and '38 Villagers in Basti Allah Wali are facing court cases filed by the Government of Pakistan on the basis of illegal occupation', where villagers say they had lived on that land more than 40 years. The attribution 'according to villagers' must be carried, because it is the letter's own.

The same letter records erosion losses at Pul Chandia, Bait Qaim Wala, Loon Wala and Parhar Ghairbi after the coffer dams were built, with no compensation for lost land, houses, tube wells, poultry and fish farms and fruit trees, and the closure of the D.G. Khan Canal from December 2005 to May 2006, after which it says 70 per cent of people shifted from Dhaundi State. These are JACSES's allegations put to the Bank as questions, not findings.

Dawn, 9 May 2006 (dateline 8 May), 'Displaced people hold demonstration: WB-funded project': the rally was held during a World Bank delegation's visit, police first blocked the protesters and they pushed through to the delegation, compensation to displaced fishermen 'ranged only from Rs16,000 to Rs40,000', and many of those displaced had still not been paid.

Dawn, 12 August 2006 (dateline Multan, 11 August), 'Demo by affectees of Taunsa Barrage': local communities asked DESCON not to work long hours at night and 'the firm allegedly did not pay heed to their request'; its staff 'reportedly started harassing residents of Allahwali Basti'; 'a case was lodged against some 15 people for allegedly hampering the construction work' and 'Two of the accused were arrested as well'. This corrects the existing case, which dates the Descon protest to August 2007 and cites a different Dawn report (news/262073).

WWF-Pakistan's baseline survey of the Taunsa Barrage Wildlife Sanctuary, submitted to the Project Management Office in August 2006: hog deer at risk of extinction within the sanctuary because the population 'was not viable and was not connected to other populations'; 'some 25 Indus Dolphins within 2.5 km of the Barrage' which 'appeared to have been displaced by the disturbance arising from project activities'; and the completion report's own sentence, 'Not all recommendations of the report were implemented' (completion report, Annex, 'Baseline Survey of the Taunsa Barrage Wildlife Sanctuary').

The two-dolphin death reported in January 2006, which WWF's final report concluded involved one dolphin, released after entanglement in a fishing net, 'although its subsequent survival was uncertain' (completion report, 'Indus Dolphin Incident').

Dawn, 24 April 2026, Alefia T. Hussain, 'The boatpeople basti who bothered a barrage': in January, 150 armed policemen and two bulldozers cleared the settlement, on 47 kanal of government land mapped as 'proposed for Circuit House'; Asad Farooq of the Alternative Law Collective says the families were moved about 2,000 feet in the first wave of evictions and 'Twenty years later, exactly what we had feared has happened'; Fazl-e-Rab of Seraiki Lok Sanjh says the government provided electricity, schools and drainage there, 'Then how is it encroachment?', and that residents had no warning; an evicted resident, Muhammad Shareef, has a pending petition against the Punjab Enforcement and Regulatory Authority, whose Director-General Ahmed Zaheer says encroachers are served a digital Emergency Prohibition Order. The authority was launched in July 2025 under a 2024 law.
corrections_made_while_checking: The draft said 'In January 2026, Dawn reported'. The article is dated 24 April 2026 and reports an operation that took place in January. Report date and event date must be given separately.

The draft said the May 2006 protest was 'at the resettlement site'. The article does not say that; it says the rally was taken out during the World Bank delegation's visit and that police first blocked it.

The draft's displaced_note attributed '157 households and 799 people' to JACSES's reading of the resettlement action plan of 29 November 2005. That figure is in neither the 26 October 2006 letter nor the English project page, which are the two JACSES files that can be read. agara-zemo-osiauri-e60-agarebi.community: The project upgraded 12 km of the E60 between the Agara bypass and the Gomi bypass at Zemo Osiauri. It acquired about 110 hectares in 571 land parcels, 40 per cent of it private land. The completion report records that 1,162 people in 272 households were affected, that five households were resettled, that four businesses stopped operating, that one construction material processing plant and 20 reservoirs were relocated within the company's own grounds, and that 20 ancillary and 45 minor structures were affected. GEL 8.2 million was paid for loss of land and crops, loss of buildings and structures, and livelihood restoration. The same paragraph records that no complaints related to land acquisition and resettlement were reported, and that the design of the second interchange was modified several times to reduce the resettlement impact. The resettlement process was completed in February 2018. The project's resettlement action plan of March 2017 gives the detail behind the five households. Thirteen residential houses were originally to be affected; a 2014 design change took all thirteen outside the resettlement corridor; the 2016 design update brought six residential houses owned by four households back under impact, and added two households with 11 affected people who had to be physically resettled, both at the second interchange. Of those two, the plan records that for one 'it was impossible to continue living in the house', and that the second 'was severally impacted as the house was damaged by construction works (the house started to get cracks, entry to the house will be blocked), hence the RD decided to relocate this AH'. The same plan lists the two operating commercial buildings lost as a boutique hotel, shop and storehouse complex and a gas filling station complex with an administrative building, boiler building, gas cylinder reception and workshops, watch building, transformer building and pumping station; their owners received one year of income compensation and replacement cost for the structures. A January 2018 addendum added one more household that was physically displaced, out of two households with seven members newly affected. Residents of Agarebi village, in the area of the second interchange, filed some 50 complaints about indirect damage from the highway works, mostly verbally, to the Roads Department and the contractor. The completion report says the Agarebi case 'took exceptionally long time to be resolved' and appears in mission reports from May 2017 onwards. Most complaints were settled quickly, with the contractor asphalting a local road, building an access road to the bus station, clearing a clogged irrigation channel and replacing damaged fences at its own expense. The complaints that took long were those about 'alleged damages (cracks) on several houses and loss of grazing land (due to loss of access) which led to reduction and eventually loss of cattle for a number of affected households'. A livelihood restoration plan giving money to the affected households was agreed with 44 of them and approved only in June 2020, six months after the loan closed.

agara-zemo-osiauri-e60-agarebi.outcome: The credit and loan closed on 31 December 2019. Resettlement was recorded as complete in February 2018, but the livelihood restoration plan for the 44 households at Agarebi whose houses cracked and whose cattle were lost was approved only in June 2020. The completion report rated the project's outcome Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rated it Moderately Satisfactory. The project also paid for feasibility studies and detailed designs for road sections to be built by other financiers, and the completion report records that this arrangement 'takes control over the quality of design documentation away from the Bank-financed project while attribution to EWHIP-4 remains'. A private agro-producing company complained to the Bank about inadequate information and consultation on pollution from construction and operation on one of those other corridors, where the environmental and social assessment had been financed by the European Investment Bank.

agara-zemo-osiauri-e60-agarebi.confidence_note: Everything here comes from the Bank's own completion report, the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it, and the project's own resettlement action plan and its addendum, which the Roads Department of Georgia prepared. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of the Agarebi village complaints was found. The completion report describes the complaints as 'mainly verbal', calls the cracks on houses 'alleged', and records that no complaints about land acquisition and resettlement were reported at all. No document found names any affected household, says how many cattle were lost, gives the amount of the June 2020 livelihood restoration payments, or says how long the Agarebi complaints went unresolved beyond the May 2017 starting point. The completion report's cover carries the date 30 September 2020. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date anywhere on its 22 pages; 26 June 2021 is the Bank document date.
agara-zemo-osiauri-e60-agarebi.conditions: The project was prepared under the Bank's safeguard policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement policy framework was disclosed in February 2012 and a resettlement action plan in March 2013, with a replacement plan for the Agara to Zemo Osiauri section in March 2017 and an addendum in January 2018. The Borrower carried out a full-scale environmental impact assessment of the upgrading. The 'future studies' component financed feasibility studies and designs for road investments by financiers other than the World Bank but did not include the environmental impact assessments those designs needed, and the completion report records that the timing and quality of those assessments 'depended on external factors and interfered with the delivery of design documents'. Resettlement policy frameworks for the Jinvali-Larsi and Kvesheti-Kobi roads and for the Rustavi-Red Bridge and Algeti-Sadakhlo roads were prepared and disclosed under this project number in 2018 for works later financed by others (Implementation Completion and Results Report, P130413).

Approved 11 June 2013, effective 16 October 2013, mid-term review 15 May 2017. The revised amount was US$109,644,887 and US$101,498,675 was disbursed. Original closing was 30 August 2019; actual closing was 30 October 2020 after four restructurings, on 9 September 2015, 29 January 2018, 30 July 2019 and 27 April 2020. The Maluku special economic zone was component 2, allocated US$27 million at approval; the Independent Evaluation Group's review gives the actual figure as 'US$6', with no unit, where it gives millions for the other components. This was a category A project triggering seven safeguard policies, including involuntary resettlement. On 13 January 2016 the Bank notified the Government that it was partially suspending disbursements under category 2.3, the physical infrastructure for the zone, for 'poor implementation of the RAP for the SEZ of Maluku and the absence of an ESMP linked to the construction by the government of a wholesale market within the zone'; the suspension was lifted on 29 March 2017, 14.5 months later. The implementing agency was the Cellule d'Exécution des Financements en faveur des États Fragiles, the unit inside the Ministry of Finance that manages Bank-financed operations in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The completion report of 30 June 2021 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Modest; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0022662 agreed on outcome and Bank performance (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00005497, 30 June 2021; IEG ICR Review ICRR0022662).

lenders.name: International Finance Corporation
lenders.role: Ran the special economic zone programme that preceded the credit, set up at the request of the Democratic Republic of the Congo's Ministry of Industry in 2008 and ended in 2012. It identified the site and delivered the master plan, the environmental and social impact assessment and the resettlement action plan for the zone. It re-engaged after the public-private partnership was signed in January 2020 to structure advisory work towards an IFC investment (Implementation Completion and Results Report, annex 8, 30 June 2021).

companies.name: MIK
companies.role: Joint venture between the Government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the South African operator Africom. The completion report records that MIK 'had already launched physical works in the SEZ for the construction of ancillary infrastructure (access road, power supply and port), although safeguards requirements had not been adhered to, particularly the RAP that was being implemented and the requirement for MIK to conduct an environmental and social screening of the site, followed by a PGES'. The works were launched under the leadership of the Prime Minister's office in charge of agro-industrial development. The Bank's implementation report of 10 April 2016 records that the market was built on a 14-hectare plot the Government allocated inside the zone while the owner of that land had not been compensated, and lifting the Bank's suspension required, among other things, that this owner be compensated (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 June 2021).

companies.name: Strategos
companies.role: International private developer with which a public-private partnership for the zone was signed officially on 28 January 2020 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, annex 8, 30 June 2021).

companies.name: Artelia
companies.role: Consultants who carried out the field census of property, the geo-referencing of dwellings and the household survey behind the 2012 resettlement action plan for the zone (Plan d'Action de Réinstallation pour la ZES de Maluku, 27 August 2012).

maluku-sez-maes-inkiene-demolition.community: The project financed basic infrastructure for a special economic zone at Maluku, at the eastern edge of Kinshasa on the Congo river. The resettlement action plan of 27 August 2012, based on an Artelia field census with a 25 July 2012 cut-off, found 58 households losing a main dwelling and 37 further rightsholders losing buildings other than main dwellings covering 2,800 square metres, losing crops, or both. The plan did not count the people in those 58 households: it surveyed 46 of them, found 431 people, an average of 9.4 a household, and applied that average to all 58 to reach 'about 545 persons to resettle', of whom it puts 302 at children. It lists the 58 households one by one by village, street and household size, with households of 24, 20, 19, 17 and 15 people among them; its table numbers 21 of them at Inkiene and 37 at Maes, while its text says 22 at Inkiene and 37 at Maes. The losses also covered 39 hectares of farms and about 20 hectares of extensive cultivation and a football pitch; a cemetery was preserved. The zone's footprint was 233 hectares, of which 11.3 hectares were inhabited. Against that plan, the completion report records that the joint venture MIK started building the access road, the power supply and the port before the resettlement plan had been carried out and before the required environmental and social screening, and that the Government separately built a wholesale market inside the zone with no environmental and social management plan. The Bank's implementation report of 10 April 2016 is more specific about what the Bank objected to: the market was built 'on a plot of 14ha allocated by the Government within the Maluku SEZ while the owner of the land has not yet been compensated'. The Bank partially suspended disbursements on the zone's infrastructure from 13 January 2016 to 29 March 2017, and the completion report gives the ground for the suspension as non-adherence to the Bank's safeguard standards 'with regard to resettlements and compensation of owners being displaced because of the establishment of the SEZ'. Compensating the owner of the land the market stood on was one of the two conditions for lifting it. The report then gives the payments: 'The PDPC, with funds from the Government, executed the payment of 622 people listed in the project area for a total amount of US$ 4,422,055.68', of which US$3,906,544.01 was for the Maluku resettlement plan. In September 2018, 49 complaints from vegetable growers who had been working inside the pilot zone were submitted to the project; the report says that after the cases were handled, 37 people were declared eligible for compensation and received it, and says nothing about the other 12. The complaints the project logged were mostly about restricted access to resources or lost revenue, resettlement of populations and compensation, and disputes over who owned a particular asset. In one of them, compensation under a resettlement plan for an electricity line was paid to a man and an accomplice who were not the owners, to the detriment of the rightful owner of the neighbouring concession at the Lunga Vasa substation; that complaint was closed in December 2018 after negotiations between the parties. The report rates environmental and social safeguards overall moderately satisfactory, and records that supervision missions found the safeguard instruments were being adhered to.
maluku-sez-maes-inkiene-demolition.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 976 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The project's own resettlement action plan of 27 August 2012 plans for 58 households losing a main dwelling; its figure of about 545 people is not a count but the plan's own extrapolation, 431 people in the 46 households it surveyed applied across all 58. The completion report's only outcome figure is the 622 people paid US$4,422,055.68 with government funds, which it describes as people 'listed in the project area' and does not break down between those who were moved and those who lost land, crops or buildings. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated at Maluku.
maluku-sez-maes-inkiene-demolition.killed_note: The completion report records that the Borrower reported around ten occupational health and safety incidents across the project's sites, most of them minor injuries to fingers or feet, and that no deaths were reported by the project unit during the whole project. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats this.
maluku-sez-maes-inkiene-demolition.outcome: The grant closed on 30 October 2020. The Bank's suspension was lifted on 29 March 2017 once the owner of the land had been compensated and an environmental and social management plan had been prepared and cleared. Of the US$27 million allocated to the zone at approval, the Independent Evaluation Group's review records the actual figure as 'US$6', printing no unit where it gives millions for the project's other components. The basic infrastructure and a 6,155-metre protective wall were built with project funds, a national special economic zone agency was set up, and a public-private partnership with the developer Strategos was signed on 28 January 2020. The completion report's own annex presents the zone as a 'Success story' and makes no mention of the resettlement, the suspension or the growers' complaints; it also gives the zone's area as 244 hectares where the resettlement plan gives the footprint as 233 hectares.

maluku-sez-maes-inkiene-demolition.confidence_note: The suspension, its dates and its stated ground, the works MIK began before the resettlement plan was carried out, the 622 people paid and the 49 growers' complaints all come from the Bank's own completion report and its implementation status report of 10 April 2016; the Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the suspension and the payment but omits the works begun before the plan and omits the growers' complaints entirely. The 58 households are from the project's own resettlement action plan of 2012 and are a plan, not an outcome, and its 545 people are an extrapolation from 46 surveyed households rather than a count. No independent account of what happened at Maes and Inkiene was found in Congolese or international reporting. No document found says how many people were actually moved, when they moved, what each household received, what became of the 12 growers who are not among the 37 the report says were paid, or who the owner of the market plot was. The completion report and its own annex give the zone's area differently, 233 hectares in the resettlement plan and 244 hectares in annex 8, and the resettlement plan's text and its own table disagree on how many of the 58 households were at Inkiene.
maluku-sez-maes-inkiene-demolition.conditions: The project was category A and triggered seven safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, pest management, physical cultural resources, involuntary resettlement, forests, and projects on international waterways, for which a riparian notification exception was granted on 1 May 2013. An environmental and social management framework, a resettlement policy framework, several impact assessments and resettlement plans and a pest management plan were prepared and disclosed through the Bank's InfoShop between 2012 and 2013, and more than 35 safeguard instruments in all were prepared over the project's life. Non-observance of the Bank's environmental and social safeguard policies led to the partial suspension of disbursements under category 2.3 from 13 January 2016 to 29 March 2017. A grievance mechanism ran through books held at Maluku's communal house and in Kongo-Central's urban, sector and territorial administrations, forms held by the works firms, and a form on the implementing unit's website (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 June 2021).

lenders.name: World Bank, as administrator of the Sierra Leone Infrastructure Development Fund
lenders.role: Grant TF-13246 of US$16 million from the Sierra Leone Infrastructure Development Fund for the Sierra Leone Energy Access Project (P126180). The fund was a multi-donor trust fund set up by the World Bank in 2010 with the UK Department for International Development as anchor donor. Approved 23 January 2013 according to the completion report's data sheet, effective 18 September 2013 against an original date of 20 September 2013. US$15.67 million was disbursed. Original closing was 31 October 2015; actual closing was 31 July 2017 after restructurings on 13 April 2017 and in October 2015, which the report's data sheet dates 29 October and its restructuring table 28 October. No mid-term review was held; the planned review of 30 June 2016 fell in the Ebola outbreak. Category B, triggering environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. The completion report of 31 January 2018 rated relevance of objectives High, outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Moderately Satisfactory, with efficiency Modest; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0021153 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory and overall Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory. The implementing agency was the Ministry of Energy, through the project management unit that also ran the Bank-financed Bumbuna project. The Bank suspended disbursement for a period to force the contractor into compliance with safeguards (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00004215, 31 January 2018; IEG ICR Review ICRR0021153).

lenders.name: UK Department for International Development
lenders.role: Anchor donor of the Sierra Leone Infrastructure Development Fund and co-financier. Its change of priorities led to the level one restructuring of October 2015, which cancelled the rural electrification component and dropped the pilot photovoltaic programme from the project (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 31 January 2018).

companies.name: British Engineering Services
companies.role: Contractor on the ground for the Freetown network upgrade. The completion report states that 'there was lack of speedy responsiveness by British Engineering Services, the contractor on the ground, in adhering to very basic safety precautions to minimize the impacts', and that there was minimal progress by the contractor after several safeguards missions and recommendations, until the matter was escalated to the Bank's Sierra Leone country management unit, the Energy Minister and the Minister of Finance and disbursement was suspended to force compliance (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 31 January 2018).

companies.name: Electricity Distribution and Supply Authority
companies.role: Sierra Leone's state electricity distribution utility, successor to the National Power Authority, which owns the Freetown distribution network the project upgraded and which prepared the 2010 resettlement plan for the same line (Abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan, 29 April 2016).

companies.name: Centre for Accountability and Rule of Law
companies.role: Sierra Leonean organisation hired by the Ministry of Energy as independent external observer of the resettlement plan's implementation (Abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan, 29 April 2016).

freetown-wellington-33kv-demolitions.community: The project rehabilitated and upgraded the 7.6 km 33/11 kV distribution line from Blackhall Road to Wellington substation in east Freetown, replacing 54 towers, in what the Ministry of Energy's own plan calls a highly congested area holding the largest number of industries in Freetown. The abbreviated resettlement action plan of 29 April 2016 states that the work 'will result in permanent displacement impacts for local communities who live and/or own business units along the 7.6km stretch', that structures breaching the right of way or safety clearances 'require full or partial demolition', and that other dwellings would be hit temporarily by excavation, concrete work and the stringing of the lines. It identifies 107 project-affected persons, of whom 81 owned structures marked for partial demolition and 26 would have their structures completely demolished. The same plan records what happened the last time the line was cleared: the National Power Authority's 2010 resettlement plan identified 23 affected people, only 22 of the 23 were compensated for properties mapped for demolition, compensation was paid on condition that people demolished their own structures afterwards, 'However, not all the PAPs complied and have continued to occupy the RoW'. A further plan prepared in 2012 was never implemented. People who had been compensated in 2010 and had not demolished or moved were entitled this time only to movement and demolition assistance and livelihood support, not to cash for their structures. The cut-off date was 31 January 2015. The plan notes that over 75 per cent of the affected people did not depend on the land for a living and a similar share would suffer only partial demolition, and that an inter-ministerial sub-committee was formed, with the Strategy and Policy Unit in the office of the President overseeing the project, 'In anticipation of any potential resistance by the current occupants to prevent the project from taking place'; the plan adds that this was done to ensure the Government and the President achieved the agenda of providing electricity in Freetown, and concludes 'As a result the chances that resistance to relocate might arise is minimal if not none'. On the outcome, the completion report states that the dismantling and stringing of towers 'resulted in additional damage to properties', that the design followed the existing right of way from an earlier project's plans, that there was minimal buffer for work space, and that the client's safeguards specialist resigned and took time to replace. It records that safeguards preparation and compensation payments 'started of satisfactorily but deteriorated to Moderately Unsatisfactory in the last months to project closure', and that the plan 'was implemented satisfactorily with only two outstanding cash compensation (totaling about 1000 USD) largely attributed to procedural bottlenecks': one person had not been present when assets were enumerated and the other case involved several claimants in court. The unit paid additional compensation during implementation to people left out, to people whose further land was needed, and for inconvenience to one person caused by the project running long. Between 65 and 70 affected people took part in a livelihood restoration programme, all of them receiving seedlings for vegetable gardening, and 68 hand washing basins, hand sanitiser and soap were handed out during the Ebola crisis. The Independent Evaluation Group adds that during preparation, compensation was paid to 164 households for moving structures out of the right of way for safety, under the resettlement plan of the earlier Bank-financed Power and Water Project.
freetown-wellington-33kv-demolitions.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 888 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Ministry of Energy's abbreviated resettlement action plan of 29 April 2016 identifies 107 project-affected persons, 26 of whom were to have their structures completely demolished and 81 partially. No Bank document found gives a count of people actually relocated, and the completion report gives no figure for how many of the 107 were paid or moved.
freetown-wellington-33kv-demolitions.outcome: The grant closed on 31 July 2017, extended from 31 October 2015, to finish the Freetown upgrade and the resettlement plan that went with it. By the end of 2016 the Freetown upgrade and its compensation and relocation were the only activities still running. At the completion report's writing, one of the two outstanding compensation payments had been made and the court case over the other was unresolved; the Ministry responsible for energy said it expected to use interest earnings on project funds to pay it once the court decided, and the remaining issues were passed to a later Bank project, the Energy Sector Utility Reform Project. The contractor resolved all compensation for damage caused during construction. The Independent Evaluation Group's lesson on this project is that 'insufficient attention on the part of both the Bank and the borrower to oversee compliance with social and environmental safeguards undermined compliance of safeguards relating to involuntary resettlement during implementation'. The report rates safeguards compliance overall Moderately Satisfactory and records the project as in compliance with social and environmental safeguards at the time the report was finalised.

freetown-wellington-33kv-demolitions.conditions: The project was category B and triggered environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. An environmental and social impact assessment and an environmental and social management plan were prepared, and the resettlement plan prepared for the same line in 2010 was updated in 2012 and again in April 2016. A four-tier grievance process ran from ward councillors at community level, through a resettlement plan implementation committee and an inter-ministerial sub-committee, to the courts. The Ministry of Energy hired the Centre for Accountability and Rule of Law as external monitor. When the contractor did not act on safeguards missions' recommendations, the matter was escalated to the Bank's country management unit, the Energy Minister and the Minister of Finance, and 'disbursement was subsequently suspended for a while to force compliance' (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 31 January 2018).

lenders.role: Grant IDA-H6830 of SDR 12.7 million, US$20.0 million equivalent, approved 17 May 2011 and effective 30 August 2011, for the Road Climate Resilience Project (P125032), with three later tranches: credit IDA-53030 of US$25.0 million, loan IBRD-82900 of US$15.0 million and credit IDA-60120 of US$35,201,256. companies.name: Marino Enterprise
companies.role: Local contractor on the Lot 2 works. The updated resettlement plan for Lot 2 records that at a public consultation in Suco Talitu a man said 'his residential structure was left hanging by the local contractor (Marino Enterprise) during the opening of bypass but it was later paid by the contractor and the AP now re-built his residential structure outside the RROW' (Updated Resettlement Plan for Lot 2, August 2018).

laulara-solerema-road-structures.community: The project rebuilt the Dili to Ainaro road in five lots. The resettlement impacts were concentrated on Lot 2, the Laulara to Solerema section. The project's updated resettlement plan for that lot, dated August 2018 and disclosed on 7 November 2018, counts 242 affected people or household heads with 1,454 household members on the old alignment, plus 11 people with 105 household members on the re-alignments. Of the 242, the plan's summary says twice that '26 APs with 146 households will be displaced since their residential structures need to be demolished to accommodate the design', while a later section of the same plan puts it at 12 affected persons with 84 households; the plan uses 'households' and 'family members' interchangeably throughout, and gives the household total as 1,454 in one place and 1,545 in another. A further 164 units of structures owned by 123 affected people were listed for demolition, of which 102 were temporary roadside stalls, called barakas, owned by 82 households; 13 permanent and 8 semi-permanent commercial structures were severely affected, along with 8 permanent, 4 semi-permanent and 8 temporary residential structures, 13 temporary kitchens, 7 permanent, 2 semi-permanent and 2 temporary toilets, 78.9 metres of concrete fence, 245 metres of temporary fence and 203 metres of cyclone wire. The residential structures severely affected on the old alignment came to 1,190.63 square metres, belonging to 34 affected people with 171 household members. The plan records that 'All the surveyed assets encroached on the land owned by the government' and that no private land had to be acquired, because the affected people occupied the government's 3 to 5 metre reserved strip. Its own view of the demolitions was that 'it is apparent that relocation is not a preference considering the available spaces for them to re-organize at the upper and/or lower portion of their present residence'. The plan also records 7,432 trees inventoried for removal along the old alignment, of which 5,364 were fruit or fruit-timber trees and 796 timber trees, and 2,847 trees already removed during the construction of re-alignments and bypasses, owned by 11 people. The outcome is in the completion report, which rates social safeguards compliance overall Satisfactory, with the Bank's safeguard requirements observed, and records that the resettlement plan for Lot 2, with its supplemental plan, 'was implemented completely with the compensation paid to all affected people (nevertheless, as noted in Aide Memoires, the execution of the Resettlement Plans for all road sections suffered delays)'. Payments on Lots 1, 3, 4 and 5 were finished except for a few cases where bank account details had to be corrected, and the total number of affected people across all five lots was 1,184, made up of 152 on Lot 1, 222 on Lot 2, 207 on Lot 3, 253 on Lot 4 and 350 on Lot 5. The report also records that 'Delay in resolving of Resettlement issues and civil grievances resulted in frequent stoppage of work by the contractor'. Fifty-three grievances were registered over the project, of which 43 were social, 6 were resettlement and 4 were environmental, health and safety matters. One incident of gender-based violence was reported and addressed by completion. A tree fell on a house in April 2022.
laulara-solerema-road-structures.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 851 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's own count of affected people across all five lots is 1,184, and it gives no count of anyone relocated. The nearest figure to a count of people moved is in the project's own updated resettlement plan for Lot 2 of August 2018, which states twice that 26 affected people with 146 households 'will be displaced since their residential structures need to be demolished', and once that the number is 12 affected people with 84 households. Those are plan figures in a plan that contradicts itself, and the plan's own view is that 'relocation is not a preference considering the available spaces for them to re-organize at the upper and/or lower portion of their present residence'. No document found counts anyone relocated, so the field is not filled.
laulara-solerema-road-structures.killed_note: The completion report records two fatal traffic incidents involving the project's workers, in August and September 2022, which 'were not reported immediately'; the Ministry of Public Works submitted root cause analysis reports for both on 23 November 2022, and the Bank then required the contractor's drivers and operators to be retrained by the supervision engineer, safety and speed limit signs and proper barricading to be installed, and a vehicle safety inspection report on all vehicles, all by 21 December 2022. Neither death is counted, because neither document states a cause for either. The report names one of them in its lessons section, where it says stone masonry guard rails 'should be improved upon or replaced with alternative materials with greater capacity to protect road users' and to retain occupants of faster or heavier vehicles 'as to avoid fatal incidents, such as the one involving a loader operator of the TLRCRP Lot 2 contractor - on August 14, 2022'; that is a recommendation about the project's guard rails, not a finding on what caused the death, and the contents of the root cause analyses are not given. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of this report records the four environmental, health and safety grievances but does not mention either fatality. Separately, the completion report notes that residents and road users raised safety concerns about the rebuilt road's higher speeds and traffic volumes and that more motorbike crashes have been seen, 'even though they reported not seeing or knowing of any fatal injuries, and most of the outcomes being minor injuries'.
laulara-solerema-road-structures.outcome: The last credit closed on 31 December 2022, seven years after the original closing date. The Lot 2 resettlement plan was recorded as implemented in full with compensation paid to all affected people, and social safeguards compliance was rated overall Satisfactory, after delays noted in mission reports on every lot and work stoppages the report attributes to unresolved resettlement issues and civil grievances. The completion report also records that a pre-construction road safety audit was commissioned for the whole corridor and for the Lot 1 design, with recommendations to be incorporated, and that these 'were not effectively implemented, nor the road safety approach fully embedded in the subsequent activities; it was a missed opportunity not making the corridor safe for every road user, especially around schools where more footpaths and traffic calming measures are needed'.

nigeria-federal-roads-trader-relocations.community: The project rehabilitated and maintained federal roads across Nigeria. The completion report states that the rehabilitated roads were built within the existing right of way 'and therefore there was minimal relocation of PAPs. Nevertheless, a total of 675 PAPs had to relocate their businesses during construction works.' Site-specific abbreviated resettlement plans were prepared road by road and give the make-up of that figure. The plan for the Akure to Ilesha road, dated October 2012 with a cut-off of 18 November 2012, counts 130 people who own structures or trade within 10 metres of the carriageway centreline and lists the losses as loss of business premises, loss of income from business premises and loss of permanent structures, with an implementation cost of N7,294,407.13 plus a 10 per cent contingency. The plan for the Gombe to Biu road counts 190 people trading within 3.65 metres of the road edge, with losses of business premises and income but no loss of permanent structures, mostly people using tables or makeshift kiosks to sell palm oil, grains, beans, tea, bread, noodles, sugar cane and black-market petrol and engine oil, and notes women who sun-dry farm produce at the roadside as a vulnerable group to be given platforms elsewhere. The plan for the Mokwa to Bida road counts 366 people. The plan for the alternate bridge at km 7+350 on the Enugu to Abakaliki road lists among the things in the way a woman's local shop, naming her as Patricia Anyanwu, along with local sand miners, a block industry, pipelines and a perimeter fence, and about 8 metres by 100 metres of Otukwu village land with economic trees on it. On what happened, the completion report says that 'Largely the owners of these businesses have been compensated and all have confirmed their satisfaction, though payments were later than expected', and then records the specific failure: 'During the April 2016 Implementation Support Mission, it was observed that the Project Affected People along Akure-Ilesha road had not been paid compensation as late as March 2016, even though the works had been completed.' The reason given is that money for resettlement was not available, partly because of problems in adopting a single treasury account in 2012. Counterpart funds were later released and the report states that payment was then made to all affected people.
nigeria-federal-roads-trader-relocations.displaced_label: 675 project-affected persons who 'had to relocate their businesses during construction works' - trading places, not dwellings (World Bank completion report, paragraph 73, 29 December 2017); the project's own road-by-road plans estimated 130 on Akure to Ilesha, 190 on Gombe to Biu and 366 on Mokwa to Bida
nigeria-federal-roads-trader-relocations.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 750 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's figure of 675 counts people who moved a business, not a home; it states that the roads were built inside the existing right of way and that relocation of affected people was minimal. The three road plans' own counts of 130, 190 and 366 are estimates made before the works for three of the five roads that had plans, and come to 686 between them; the completion report gives 675 for the project as a whole and no road-by-road outcome count, so the two sets of figures are not measuring the same thing.
nigeria-federal-roads-trader-relocations.outcome: The credit closed on 30 June 2017. The completion report states that with every affected person compensated, compliance with the Bank's social safeguard policy was rated satisfactory, and that environmental compliance was initially weak but improved with additional oversight by Bank specialists. The project's own outcome was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory by both the completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group. The road fatality rate it was meant to cut from 161 to 120 deaths per 10,000 vehicles reached 143.

nigeria-federal-roads-trader-relocations.confidence_note: The 675 people who moved their businesses, the unpaid compensation on the Akure to Ilesha road in March 2016 after the works were finished, and the reason given for it all come from the Bank's own completion report; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report repeats them. The road-by-road counts come from the Federal Ministry of Works' own resettlement plans, which are plans and not records of what was done. No independent account of these roadside traders was found; one academic study of traders displaced by road widening in Akure covers the Arakale road, a different, state-financed project of 2010 to 2011. No document found says how many people on the Akure to Ilesha road were unpaid, how long they waited, what any of them received, or whether the women who sun-dried produce beside the Gombe to Biu road were ever given the platforms the plan promised. The completion report also states that all the business owners 'have confirmed their satisfaction' and that payment was eventually made to all of them.
nigeria-federal-roads-trader-relocations.conditions: A resettlement policy framework was prepared and disclosed before appraisal. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that 'The project was not expected to result in loss of land. However, a Resettlement Policy Framework (RPF) was prepared in case relocation of' people proved necessary, with a detailed resettlement plan to follow the detailed design of each road. Site-specific abbreviated plans were then prepared and disclosed for the Akure to Ilesha, Gombe to Biu, Mokwa to Bida, Enugu to Abakaliki and Ogoja to Ikom roads in 2010 and 2012, with environmental management plans for the periodically maintained roads. The 2 February 2011 restructuring changed the project's legal covenants. The report gives the non-availability of funds for resettlement, partly from the adoption of a single treasury account by the federal government in 2012, as the reason compensation went unpaid after works were complete (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 29 December 2017; IEG ICR Review ICRR0021110).

lenders.name: Global Environment Facility, through the World Bank
lenders.role: Grant TF-53110 of US$5.5 million for the Greater Addo Elephant National Park Project (P064438). Approved 24 February 2004, effective 28 June 2004 against an original date of 30 April 2004, mid-term review 21 May 2007. The revised amount and the amount disbursed were both US$5.3 million. Original closing was 30 April 2010; actual closing was 30 October 2010 after a six-month extension requested in 2009. Environmental category B and global focal area B. The project triggered three safeguard policies, environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. The implementing agency was South African National Parks. The Bank was responsible for approving the resettlement action plan. The completion report of 27 April 2011 rated outcome Satisfactory, risk to the global environment outcome Low or Negligible, Bank performance Satisfactory and borrower performance Highly Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR13655, posted 7 November 2013, rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Moderate. The mid-term review cut the target for terrestrial area under park management from 236,000 to 205,000 hectares and for private land under contractual arrangement from 46,000 to 30,000 hectares, and the grant agreement was amended to match (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00001883, 27 April 2011; IEG ICR Review ICRR13655, 7 November 2013).

companies.name: South African National Parks
companies.role: The statutory national parks agency of South Africa and the project's implementing agency, which bought the farms, prepared and ran the resettlement policy framework and resettlement action plan, and chaired the quarterly Resettlement Working Group. addo-park-farm-worker-rehousing.community: The project paid for the expansion of the Addo Elephant National Park by buying farms from willing sellers in the Sundays River Valley. The resettlement action plan of 17 June 2003 sets out whose homes those farms were. It records that during phase 1, for 13 farms, 'it is estimated that 165 workers and an additional 544 dependants will fall within the ambit of the RPF', and that on the 6 priority farms surveyed there were 35 farm workers and 34 dependants, 69 inhabitants in all, averaging 3.3 people and 1.7 workers to a household. It describes the people: 84 per cent aged 18 to 49, 73 per cent men, 24 per cent with no education at all and only 13 per cent with any secondary schooling, 63 per cent having worked only on farms, median income R588 a month. It records that a large part of their income came in kind - meat, staple foods, water, limited electricity, firewood, housing, clothing, limited transport, loans and the right to keep livestock on the farm - benefits that did not stop at retirement, so that 'the elderly have a safety net provided by the farmer. Once displaced from the farn, such benefits would fall away.' The plan answers its own concern, undertaking that South African National Parks 'will ensure that incomes are replaced via the income restoration strategy outlined in this document'. It states the concern plainly: 'concern has been expressed that farm workers would be likely to lose access to employment and places of accommodation typically provided on the farms. Farm workers are regarded as among the most vulnerable members of South Africa's working class'. The outcome, in the completion report, is that the plan and its socio-economic programme were prepared 'to resettle 29 households or Project Affected Persons (PAP) in two surrounding municipalities (Sundays River Valley and Blue Crane) and to help the displaced individuals to recover their overall livelihoods', and that of those 29, 'A group of 11 households were moved to municipal houses, another group of 10 households were moved to houses provided by SANParks and a last group of 8 households have not been moved.' On the eight, the Bank's social safeguards specialist visited the municipal government and was shown a council resolution letter putting all of them on the Reconstruction and Development Programme housing list on a priority basis, with houses to be built on their plots when each municipality's next housing project started. 'One RAP individual is not on the (RDP) housing list for Blue Crane Municipality and has chosen not to respond to assistance offers by RDP.' On the 21 who had moved, the report states that the Bank's social safeguards specialist visited the new houses 'and was satisfied with these arrangements as all the affected households were in better housing conditions than before the move'. Everyone affected was given either a job in one of the park's management programmes or a grant under the project's small, medium and micro-enterprise scheme. Teresa Connor's field study of the same park expansion, published in Development Southern Africa in 2005, records the mechanism: the park 'has subsequently been purchasing properties on a “willing seller/willing buyer” basis, which requires that a farm be cleared of all previous inhabitants upon transfer to a new owner', and notes the loss of small stock farms to conservation enterprises 'of which the GAENP is the major player'.
addo-park-farm-worker-rehousing.displaced_label: 11 households moved into municipal houses and 10 into houses provided by South African National Parks, with 8 of the 29 households the plan covered not moved by the project's close (World Bank completion report, 27 April 2011). No document prints a total of those moved, so none is given here.
addo-park-farm-worker-rehousing.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 709 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report records that the resettlement action plan was written for 29 households, that 11 were moved into municipal houses, 10 into houses provided by South African National Parks and that 'a last group of 8 households have not been moved'. The Independent Evaluation Group's review opens with '29 households were resettled' and then gives the same three groups, saying the 8 'are scheduled to move to housing projects but are waiting for relocation', so the two documents record the same outcome in different words. The project's own resettlement action plan of 2003 estimated that 165 workers and 544 dependants on 13 farms would fall within the resettlement policy framework in phase 1 alone, against the 29 households the plan was eventually written for.
addo-park-farm-worker-rehousing.outcome: The grant closed on 30 October 2010. Of the 29 households, 11 had moved into municipal houses and 10 into houses South African National Parks provided, and the Bank's social safeguards specialist recorded all of them as better housed than before. Eight were still waiting, on a municipal housing list, for houses to be built when the next housing projects began, and one person was not on the list at all. An independent audit of the resettlement plan's implementation, ordered early in 2010, concluded that South African National Parks had met its obligations to the 29, and the Bank's last social safeguards supervision mission, in May 2010, agreed. The park's terrestrial area reached 170,115 hectares against a revised target of 205,000, and 17,608 hectares of private land were brought in under contractual arrangement against a revised target of 30,000, because land prices rose from between R1,080 and R1,315 a hectare in 2003 and 2004 to between R7,000 and R8,817 a hectare by 2010 and some owners would not sell. An 11,000-hectare conservation agreement with the Enon Bersheba community did not happen, because the state had not transferred the title to the community.

addo-park-farm-worker-rehousing.confidence_note: The 29 households, the split into 11, 10 and 8, the one person off the housing list and the finding that those who moved were better housed than before all come from the Bank's own completion report, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats them. That is the lender reporting on its own project, and nothing outside the Bank reports on these 29 households. The description of the farm workers and the loss of their in-kind income comes from South African National Parks' own resettlement action plan of 2003, which is a plan and which undertakes that their incomes would be replaced. Teresa Connor's field study of the same park expansion, in Development Southern Africa in 2005, corroborates the mechanism - the park 'has subsequently been purchasing properties on a “willing seller/willing buyer” basis, which requires that a farm be cleared of all previous inhabitants upon transfer to a new owner' - but gives no count of farms or workers displaced and does not report on the households the Bank's plan covered. No document found names any of the 29 households, says when they moved, says what they were paid, or says whether the eight households still waiting in 2010 ever got houses. The independent audit of the resettlement plan that the completion report relies on, by South African National Parks in 2010, is listed as unpublished and was not found. The completion report's cover is dated 27 April 2011 and its own data sheet gives the report date as 28 April 2011.
addo-park-farm-worker-rehousing.conditions: The project triggered environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement policy framework was completed during preparation in 2003 and a resettlement action plan followed on 17 June 2003, with an abbreviated resettlement plan in 2006; the Bank was responsible for approving the plan. A Resettlement Working Group met quarterly to monitor the policy's application and its minutes are available. South African National Parks set aside enough of its own budget to cover all the costs the plan anticipated. South African legislation, the Bank's physical cultural resources policy and the agency's own heritage policies produced a Cultural Resource Framework in 2003 with a detailed inventory of cultural resources. South Africa's Extension of Security of Tenure Act and Land Reform (Labour Tenants) Act protect farm dwellers' and labour tenants' security of tenure and are cited in the resettlement plan's legal section (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 April 2011; Resettlement Action Plan, 17 June 2003).
